content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.9. I spent 27 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, `L1-S1-M1` and `L2-S2-M2`. Then I tested two tasks where the hypotheses predict opposite results:
- **`L1-S2-M2`:** every rule in it was already trained, but its responses match neither trained task on any input (0.0 overlap). Part-based predicts it's cheap to learn; holistic predicts it's expensive.
- **`L4-S3-M4`:** all three of its rules are new, but its responses match `L1-S1-M1` on 56% of inputs. Part-based predicts it's expensive; holistic predicts it's cheaper.

**Results** (examples needed to reach criterion; lower means easier):

| Task | New rules | Overlap with trained | Results | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `L1-S2-M2` | 0 | 0.0 | 19, 19, 39, 1, 20, 13, 15, 1 | ~16 |
| `L4-S3-M4` | 3 | 0.56 | 41, 64, 46, 34, 52, 40, 44, 57 | ~47 |
| `L3-S3-M3` (control) | 3 | ≤0.19 | 41, 46 | ~44 |

The two sets of results don't overlap at all. The task made only of known rules was easy even though its mapping was completely unlike anything trained. The task with all-new rules was about as hard as the dissimilar control, so its 56% overlap didn't help. Cost follows the number of new rules, not how similar the mapping is, which is what part-based predicts.

The tests are very noisy: the same task gave anywhere from 1 to 48 examples. Because of that, I couldn't tell where a task with one new rule falls (`L1-S3-M2` gave 48, 1 and 33). That's why I put confidence at 0.9 rather than higher, even though the main comparison is clear.
